title: First teachers
hook: parents are called first teachers, worthy of honor (Itivuttaka 106)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man drifting downstream, a voice from the bank, and your line, a stroke toward the bank. Did you heed one warning? Today the Itivuttaka turns from the river to the family home. Day six hundred thirty-two.

Who taught you to hold a spoon? Nobody remembers the lesson, but somebody gave it, probably more than once, probably with a towel nearby. Before any school, any book, any teacher with a title, there was a pair of hands showing you how the world works: this is hot, this is a cat, this is how you say thank you. One short discourse in the Itivuttaka gives those hands a name. It gives them a teacher's title. Today: first teachers.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO HOLD A SPOON?` → `BEFORE ANY SCHOOL.` → `A TITLE FOR THOSE HANDS.`

segments.voice: The discourse is Itivuttaka 106. The Buddha says that a family where mother and father are honored at home lives with Brahma, the high god of that world. It lives with the first teachers. It lives with those worthy of gifts. Then he unpacks the names. These, he says, are terms for mother and father. And he gives the reason in one plain sentence, paraphrased here: parents do much for their children. They bring them up, they feed them, and they show them this world. Show them this world. That's the job description of a first teacher. Not doctrine, not scripture. The world itself: a face, a word, a door, a road. The Pali for first teachers is pubbacariya: pubba, earlier, and acariya, teacher. A teacher's title, and here it goes to the people in the kitchen. The verse at the end gets practical. The wise honor them with food and drink, with clothes and a place to sleep, by bathing them and washing their feet. Care for the body that once cared for yours. Two honest things belong beside this text. First, it speaks of parents as they are meant to be, the ones who raise, feed and show. Not everyone had that, and the text doesn't pretend to describe every home. Some Buddhist teachers widen it to whoever did that work for you: a grandmother, an aunt, a neighbor, a foster parent. Second, the same idea runs through the Buddha's teaching to Sigala, where a grown child supports the parents who once supported them. Honor, here, isn't a feeling first. It's food, clothing, a place to rest.
screen: `MOTHER AND FATHER, HONORED AT HOME` · `THEY SHOW THEIR CHILDREN THIS WORLD` · `PUBBACARIYA: TEACHER FROM THE START` · `FOOD, CLOTHES, A PLACE TO REST` · then, large: `FIRST TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one person who showed you this world when you were small. A parent, if that's who it was, or a grandparent, an elder, anyone who fed you and named things for you. Picture one ordinary thing they taught you, the spoon, the shoelace, the way to say sorry. Stay with that picture and let a quiet thank you sit in the chest. If they're living, after the bell you might send them a short message. If they're gone, the thanks can stay right here. The bell holds the time.
First teachers. Pubbacariya: in Itivuttaka 106, a name for mother and father, who raise, feed, and show their children this world. Today's word.
Your line: show them this world. Thank one parent or elder today for one small thing they taught you, in a call, a note, or just in your head. Day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: In some Buddhist households, especially in Theravada countries, children bow to their parents on special days, and families make offerings or give food to monks in their parents' names as a way of honoring them.

fork.setup: the Buddha gives parents high titles, Brahma and first teachers among them. what reason does he give?
options: they are older than their children.
they bring up, feed, and show their children this world.
fork.reveal: the reason is the work they did: raising, feeding, and showing the child the world. the honor follows the care.

original.note: Pali pubbacariya: first or earliest teacher, from pubba, earlier, and acariya, teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: first teachers means your first schoolteacher.
what it means: in Itivuttaka 106, mother and father, who raise, feed, and show their children this world.

what a scholar hears: the same sutta, calling parents Brahma, first teachers and worthy of gifts, appears in the Anguttara Nikaya too; since Brahma was revered as a high god in the brahmin tradition, some readers see the title as moving sacred honor into the household.

notes: Itivuttaka 106 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the three titles (Brahma, pubbacariya, ahuneyya / worthy of gifts) and the reason given: parents are of great help, they bring up, nourish, and show their children this world.
Confirm the verse's list of service: food and drink, clothing, bedding, anointing, bathing, washing the feet.
Confirm the parallel sutta in the Anguttara Nikaya (AN 3.31 and/or AN 4.63, Sabrahmaka).
The widening to grandparents, foster parents and others is described as what many teachers do; a Keeper may prefer different wording for listeners with painful family histories.
The DN 31 duty of supporting parents is paraphrased.

Reviewer: the trapdoor had stated as settled that the Brahma title 'quietly moves sacred honor into the household'; softened to 'many readers see the title as...'. Confirm the framing is fair to the brahmin tradition.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the fork's count of 'three titles' (Iti 106 may list four names, including pubbadevata, first devas; AN 3.31 has three); cut the unsourced history of the acariya's status; 'many' softened to 'some' in teach, howItsDone and trapdoor. Keeper: confirm how many titles Iti 106 gives.
